newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD says Kohl has no plan to end solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: SPD says Kohl has no plan to end solidarity tax.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl has no plan to end the unpopular solidarity tax by the year 2000 despite an earlier pledge to do so, opposition Social Democrat (SPD) fiscal policy spokesman Joachim Poss said on Monday.

"The government has withdrawn the chancellor's promise, to meet the Maastricht fiscal criteria," Poss said, citing a letter addressed to him from state secretary for finance Hansgeorg Hauser. "The solidarity tax will continue to be collected beyond 1999."

Kohl said in a television interview last August he believed the solidarity tax, aimed at helping finance the reconstruction of formerly communist east Germany, would be done away with by the year 2000.
In subsequent statements, however, Kohl has been more guarded, saying in January for example it was too soon to set a date for the elimination of the solidarity tax.
Kohl's government and the SPD have been facing off over the future of a broader tax reform, of which cuts in the solidarity tax are one element.

Both sides agree tax cuts are needed to stimulate the economy and boost jobs, but they are wrangling publicly over specific cuts and the timing, in what many see as positioning ahead of the 1998 elections.

Hauser, in his letter to Poss, said an elimination of the solidarity tax in January 1999 "cannot be accomplished, in budgetary terms. The surcharge should however be reduced as quickly as possible and finally eliminated."

A two percentage point cut in the solidarity tax in January 1998 was decided last fall. Finance Minister Theo Waigel then appropriated it as the centrepiece of his comprehensive tax reform, aimed at reducing taxes by a net 30 billion marks ($17.7 billion).

Hauser said the timing of further cuts will be decided after the impact of the full tax reform is studied. Planned reductions in income tax rates should reduce the burden of the solidarity surcharge, he said.
Poss said, "The government does not want to say clearly in what steps and by what time it plans to reduce the solidarity tax further."
Poss said the tax reform will lead to a greater reduction in tax revenues that previously foreseen, leaving a 160 billion mark ($94.4 billion) financing gap in the years 1999-2001.
Continued economic sluggishness and high unemployment are pushing Germany's deficit higher, hampering its efforts to meet the criteria for European monetary union, he said.
-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750 ($ = 1.695 German Marks)
